To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) patients with HIV disease have an increased prevalence of prolonged QTc interval compared to a general hospital population; (2) three of 42 hospitalized patients with HIV infection demonstrated an acquired form of long QT syndrome; and (3), in our three patients with HIV disease, QTc prolongation was refractory to left stellate blockade, stress testing, and β‐blocker administration, and was responsive to mexiletine.

QTc prolongation is more common in patients with HIV disease than in the general population, that the QTc prolongation in patients with HIV may represent an unrecognized form of the acquired long QT syndrome, that torsades de pointe may be associated with QTc prolongaion in patients with HIV, and that the use of mexiletine hydrochloridewas effective in preventing torsades de pointees in patients with HIV.

QTc prolongation was more common among hospitalized patients with HIV infection than a general hospital population, and may be due to an acquired form of long QT syndrome in some patients with HIV disease.
